about: One table for the server, the app and the helper. The helper reads scripts with PowerShell's own parser; everything else here says how Rig's TypeScript reader sees a script, so the helper can match it. The vectors file holds examples of each rule, for scripts (`script`, `as`) and for whole steps (`cmd`).

Text: a script is refused when it is empty or only spaces, longer than `maxLength` characters (UTF-16 code units), or holds any character in `disguised` (hex ranges, inclusive). Case is folded for ASCII A-Z only, and only space, tab, CR and LF count as spaces; `disguised` holds the letters that fold into ASCII in .NET (U+017F, U+0130, U+0131, U+212A), so ASCII folding can't be tricked. CR LF and lone CR read as LF.

Commands: a command's name is folded. A name with \ or / is pathed: it must start with a `roots.known` entry and hold no `..`. The last part is the base; `exeSuffixes` are cut from its end, and then a base with a dot is a script file, refused. A base that is neither pathed nor had a suffix cut is looked up in `aliases` first. An entry with `exe` matches a base of that name whether pathed or not; one without `exe` matches only a plain name. With no entry: a read refuses it, a pathed program under `roots.unknown` is tier 2 with admin, any other pathed one is refused, and a plain Verb-Noun takes its tier from `verbs` (anything else is refused). In a change, such a Verb-Noun is refused when any argument is hidden, when a written-out argument (or a parameter's value joined after a colon) has a `..` part, when one whose place is registry or file holds a `paths.wildcards` character, and, when its verb is in `writerVerbs`, when one whose place is registry or file ends with one of `paths.programs`.

Arguments: an argument is a switch when written plain and it starts with - and a letter, -- and a letter, or / and a letter or ?. A parameter is - and a name, followed by a colon or the end of the word; text joined after the colon is its value. A comma between arguments only separates them (`a,b` is two arguments). An argument written as text with a variable or expression straight after it (`key=$x`) is that text, then a hidden argument. A variable, an expression, a double-quoted string with $ in it, or anything with a member or index after it is hidden. A redirection (`>`, `2>`, `*>` with its target) is not an argument, wherever it is written, as in PowerShell's own parser; a redirect to `$null` writes nothing, any other target is a write to that file. A script block's insides are read as more commands, and the block itself is not an argument.

Rules: a command's outcome is the first `when` rule that matches, else tier 0 if a `read` form matches, else the entry itself. `starts`: the first arguments equal these. `has`: some argument equals one. For an entry without `exe`, a `starts` or `has` item that begins with - matches only an argument that is a parameter (a quoted '-Program' is a value). `prefix`: some argument starts with one, or, for an argument that starts with - or /, the part before any colon is at least two characters and one listed starts with it (PowerShell's short forms: -co fits -comp). `contains`: some argument contains one. `piped`: the command takes its input from the command before it in a pipeline. `after`: the tests look only at the values of the listed parameters (the next argument, or the text after a colon), with short forms fitting both ways. For a `never`, `refused` or tier 3 rule, a hidden argument counts as a match for starts, has and contains, and for prefix when the entry is `exe` or the rule has `after` (a program gets text, so a hidden argument could be anything; a cmdlet's hidden argument can only be a value). `params` is a positive grammar for a rule that allows: no argument is hidden, and every argument after the `starts` ones that begins with - or / (the part before any colon) is one of `params`, written in full; an empty list allows none. `single`: no list and nothing positional: every argument after the `starts` ones that isn't a parameter comes right after a parameter that has no value joined after its colon. `fit`: each listed parameter (short forms fitting both ways) is given only values that match its pattern in full, folded: the text after its colon and each argument that isn't a parameter after it, up to the next parameter (patterns use only syntax JavaScript and .NET read alike). `use`: the rule applies only to a script used as one of these (read, run, undo); in any other script it is passed over.

Reads: a read form passes when the arguments begin with `starts`, include one of `has` when it is given, and every later argument that begins with - or / (the part before any colon) is in `params`, in `readParams`, or begins with one of `prefix`; short forms don't count here. `free` lets any written-out arguments follow, but no hidden one. `bare`: nothing may follow `starts`, not even a value. `literal`: in a read every argument must be written out, and the command may not take pipeline input. `blocks`: every argument that isn't a switch must be a script block.

Targets: `targets` says what a command acts on. With `at`, the arguments at those positions (counting from 0, script blocks and the redirection `>` left out). Otherwise every argument that is not a parameter, plus the value after a parameter in `paths.literal` or one that `paths.literalPrefix` starts with (at least two characters), which is a literal target; the value after a parameter listed exactly in `values` or in `paths.values` (for every command) is skipped, the value after one listed exactly in `names` or `renames` is skipped when it is written out, of kind name, holds no `paths.wildcards` character and, for a `places` command, doesn't end with one of `paths.programs` (otherwise it is a target like any other), and an argument in `paths.constants` is never a target. A skipped name is joined to the place of each registry or file target: after it with \ for `names` (what the command makes or sets inside it), or in place of its last part for `renames` (the new name beside it). With `leaves`, each registry or file target is also joined to the last part of each other one (a copy or move can land inside it under that name). The joined places are written places too, and are held to `neverText`, `protectText` and `adminText` like the script. A target's place: fold, / as \, runs of \ as one, drop a leading `Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\`, `Registry::` or `FileSystem::`, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, HKEY_USERS and HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG as hkcu, hklm, hkcr, hku and hkcc, a hive followed by : or :\ as the hive and \, and no \ at the end. Its kind: registry (a hive, alone or with \), file (a letter, :\), drive (two or more letters and :), relative (has \ or :), or name.

Target checks, in every script: a target that isn't literal and holds a `paths.wildcards` character is refused (not for kind service); a place with a `..` part is refused. In a read, a `literal` command taking pipeline input is refused, and a kind outside `paths.readKinds` is refused. In a change, for `write`: a hidden target is refused, a relative one or a bare name is refused (`relative`: PowerShell would put it in the folder the script starts in), and at least one must be registry, file or drive. `content`: every target must be a file under one of `paths.readRoots` (`*` stands for one folder name; the place must be inside the root, and end with one of `ends` when given), with at least one target. `places`: in a change no target may end with one of `paths.programs`. A redirect target in a change is held to the same wildcard, `..`, program and hidden rules, and must be a file named in full (`relative` otherwise).

Programs a script wrote: in a change, a pathed command is refused when another command of tier 1 or more has a written-out argument with \ or / whose place is the program, its folder, or a folder inside or holding it, or when another such command has no `targets`, a hidden argument and isn't a read; a redirect target counts as such an argument. A plain `exe` command is refused when such a place ends with its name and one of `exeSuffixes`, or is `paths.system`.

Constructs: a script is refused for any find in `always`, a `static` member of a type literal not in `safeStatics` (written type::member or type.member, folded, without a leading system.), or any variable in `engine` (with any scope). In a read it is also refused for a type, a method call, a redirect or setting a member (`member-assign`). In a change, a type in `safeTypes` and a method in `safeMethods` are allowed, a redirect and setting a member are allowed with a reason, and any other type or method is refused. `pinned`: variables no script may assign, and no command may be given as an argument, with any scope or an env: or variable: drive in front. Finds: `unc` is any text whose \ and / read as \ holds \\ after a web address's scheme (two or more letters and :, not file:) is dropped; `provider` is text with alias:, function: or variable: at its start or after a \; `short-name` is a letter or digit, ~ and a digit.

Text rules: `neverText` and `protectText` are tested against the script, each joined place and each touch after: fold; hkey_local_machine to hklm and hkey_current_user to hkcu; / to \; remove ` ' " + : and spaces; runs of \ become one. `neverText` refuses (reads are held only to entries with `applies` any); `protectText` makes a change tier 3. `adminText` makes a change need admin.

Remote: a command that is not pathed, had no `exeSuffixes` suffix cut and has no entry with `exe` is refused with `remote.refused` (written "Rig won't run <name>: it <refused>.") in a read, run or undo, listed or not, when any argument that is a switch or a parameter has a part before any colon that is at least two characters and either starts with one of `remote.params` or is the start of one (the short forms `prefix` matches: -co, -cims, -cred). For a listed command this comes right after its `when` rules, so a matching `when` rule that refuses or is `never` wins; for a command with no entry it comes before every test but those on its name.

Steps: a step's touches are checked before its scripts: a registry key must start with HKCU or HKLM (as HKCU\, HKCU:\, HKEY_CURRENT_USER\ or Registry:: before any of those) and is stored as HKCU\ or HKLM\; a registry `value` must be a string; a file path must start with a letter and :\ with no `..` part and no short name; no touch may hold \\ or a wildcard. Each touch is held to `neverText` and `protectText`. A step's tier is the highest of its read, run and undo. `undo: null` is no undo. With no undo the step is tier 3 unless every touch is a registry key, file or service, there is at least one, and every write in `run` is covered: each place it writes (registry and file targets of a `write`, `places` or `content` command and their joined places, service names, redirect targets) is a touch of the same kind or inside one. A write with no such place (a command without `targets`, a hidden or drive target) is never covered. A touch that no write in `run` reaches (either inside the other) adds an `unused-touch` reason. A command in `undo` whose rule has `undoes` must take back a command of the same entry in `run`: one whose first argument is one of `undoes` and whose next arguments equal this command's arguments after its first, as many as its rule's `starts` has after the first and one more (the app's id). Otherwise the step is tier 3 with the `unpaired-undo` reason. A file touch is also refused when it holds / anywhere, or any part between \ is . or .. or ends with a dot or a space (Windows strips those, so the text would name another file); the helper also requires Windows' full form of the path to be the path itself.

Running: an entry with `person` runs only as the person: a step whose read, run or undo uses it and that needs admin rights is refused (`as-person`), and the helper never runs it elevated. `minutes` is how long the helper lets a run or undo script that uses the command go on (two minutes otherwise). `expects`, on a `when` rule, names never-list places (sentinels) a command it matches may change, such as the services, Run values and tasks an installer adds. A script's waived places are those of its commands only when every command in it of tier 1 or more matched a rule with `expects` (an empty list adds none); otherwise none are waived. The helper lists waived hits on the result instead of putting them back. A step whose run has a command matched by a rule with `expects` installs, updates or uninstalls an app: when it fails, times out or trips another sentinel, and its read prints something else than before (the app changed), the helper runs the step's undo before it puts the rest back; when the read is the same it never runs the undo; when there is no undo or it fails, the waived places are listed, not put back.

File edits (`fileEdit`): the path follows the file touch rules above and the `paths.programs` check. Its ending (from the last . in its last part, folded) must be listed for the edit's format in `formats`. Its place (as a target's place) is refused when it contains any `never` entry's text, and the edit is tier 3 when it contains any `tier3` entry's text, with that entry's `says` as a reason. An `at` part may hold no character in `at` or `hidden`; an INI value no character in `iniValue` or `hidden`; a JSON string value none in `hidden` (hex ranges, inclusive).

remote.refused: would act on another computer or as another account

constructs.unreadable: Rig can't read this script, so it won't run it
constructs.characters: This script uses curly quotes, long dashes or hidden characters that can disguise a command
constructs.too-long: This script is too long for Rig to check
constructs.empty: There is no script to check
constructs.dynamic: This script works out a command's name while it runs, so Rig can't tell what it would do
constructs.dot-source: This script loads another script into itself, which Rig can't check
constructs.obfuscated: A command's name is split up with backticks or quotes, which hides what it is
constructs.splat: This script passes arguments hidden in a variable, so Rig can't see them
constructs.keyword: Rig can't check scripts that define their own functions or use this keyword
constructs.provider-variable: This script reads or writes through a ${drive:path} variable, which Rig can't classify
constructs.dynamic-member: This script calls something on an object by a name worked out while it runs
constructs.stray: This script has a word Rig can't place
constructs.unc: This script reaches for another computer over the network, or has \\ or // in a path
constructs.type: This script uses .NET directly, and Rig can't tell what that would do
constructs.method: This script calls a method on an object, and Rig can't tell what that would do
constructs.redirect: This script writes its output to a file
constructs.path: This runs a program from outside C:\Windows\System32 and C:\Program Files
constructs.script-file: This runs another script or file that Rig can't read
constructs.unknown: Rig doesn't know this command, so it can't say what it would do
constructs.unknown-program: runs a program Rig doesn't know; Rig can't say what it changes
constructs.not-read: Rig only looks with the commands on its read list, and this isn't on it
constructs.not-literal: When Rig is only looking, paths have to be written out in full, not held in a variable
constructs.member-by-name: ForEach-Object is only allowed with a script block, because a bare name can call a method
constructs.touch: The list of what this changes has an entry Rig can't use; registry keys start with HKLM\ or HKCU\ and files with a drive letter
constructs.no-undo: There is no undo script, and Rig can't snapshot everything this touches
constructs.tainted: This can't be undone, and Rig has read text from outside in this chat, so it won't offer it
constructs.pinned: This script changes what decides which program or parameters a command really gets ($env:Path, $env:PSModulePath, $env:PATHEXT or $PSDefaultParameterValues), so Rig can't be sure what would run
constructs.provider: This script reaches commands or variables through the Alias:, Function: or Variable: drive, which can change what a command does
constructs.short-name: This script uses a short name such as PROGRA~1, which hides the real path
constructs.static: This script uses .NET directly, and Rig can't tell what that would do
constructs.static-variable: This script calls .NET through a type held in a variable, so Rig can't tell what it would do
constructs.member-assign: This script sets a property on an object directly, which Rig can't describe
constructs.engine: This script reaches into PowerShell itself, which can change what other commands do
constructs.wildcard: This names a place with *, ? or [ ], which can match places Rig would refuse; use -LiteralPath or write the name out
constructs.dots: This names a place with .. in it; write the full path instead
constructs.piped-read: When Rig is only looking, this command must name what it reads itself, not take it from the command before it
constructs.read-kind: When Rig is only looking, it reads only files and the registry, named in full
constructs.not-literal-change: This changes a place or value whose name is worked out while the script runs, so Rig can't check it; write it out in full
constructs.full-path: Rig only changes files and registry keys named by their full path, such as C:\... or HKCU:\...
constructs.relative: This names a place without its full path, so it would land in whatever folder the script starts in; write it out in full, such as C:\... or HKCU:\..., and give names and values with -Name and -Value
constructs.read-place: Rig only reads files from Windows' logs, program folders, and the .log and .txt files apps keep in ProgramData and AppData
constructs.program-file: Rig doesn't copy, move or write program files, scripts or shortcuts
constructs.wrote-program: This runs a program from a place the same script changes, so it may not be the program Rig looked up
constructs.unused-touch: Rig expected each listed place to change, but the change script doesn't write there for
constructs.unpaired-undo: The undo uninstalls an app that this change doesn't install, so Rig can't be sure undo only takes back this change
constructs.as-person: This uses a program that runs only as you, never with admin rights, so it can't be in the same change as something that needs them; ask for them as separate changes

verbSays: reads something (Rig doesn't know this command by name)
changes a setting (Rig doesn't know this command by name)
removes, stops or resets something (Rig doesn't know this command by name)

neverText.says: Rig never reads saved passwords, keys, sign-in stores or the Windows account database
Rig never reads the Windows sign-in settings, which can hold a saved password
Rig never shows saved Wi-Fi passwords
Rig never reads BitLocker recovery keys
Rig never downloads code and runs it, or unpacks hidden text into commands
Rig never changes what starts with Windows through the Run keys or the Startup folder; the startup apps fix does that safely
Rig never touches Image File Execution Options or SilentProcessExit, which can swap one program for another or start one when another closes
Rig never changes the Windows sign-in hooks
Rig never changes what runs when you sign in or open a command prompt
Rig never changes which program opens programs, scripts or Settings
Rig never turns on keeping sign-in passwords in memory (WDigest)
Rig never changes where Windows finds programs and their parts

Rig never changes the other places that start a program by themselves: sign-in and startup scripts, the old Load and Run values, the crash debugger, Windows setup's command and files swapped at restart
Rig never adds code that Windows loads into other programs or services (AppCertDlls, print monitors and providers, network providers, AMSI providers)
Rig never changes the environment every program starts with, which decides where Windows finds programs, or where Windows keeps your folders, the Startup folder among them
Rig never changes which program a service runs, as whom, or what it runs when it fails
Rig never changes the hosts file, or where Windows looks for it
Rig never points this PC's proxy somewhere else
Rig never adds Defender exclusions
Rig never adds trusted root certificates
Rig never turns on ways into this PC from outside (Remote Desktop, WinRM, an SSH server, Remote Registry)
Rig never changes User Account Control, the Windows prompt its own approvals rely on
Rig never changes its own files, log or guard
Rig never changes how Windows starts, which can stop this PC booting

protectText.says: It changes Microsoft Defender's settings or policy, which can turn protection off
It changes SmartScreen, Core isolation, Credential Guard or Safe Mode
It changes the Windows firewall's policy
It changes how one of Windows' security services starts (Defender, the firewall, Security Center, the event log, Windows Update or AppLocker)
It lowers the protection on files from the internet (attachment and internet zone settings)
It changes when Office runs macros
It changes which scripts PowerShell will run
It changes the list of programs Windows blocks
It changes which program the screen saver runs
It changes which program code Windows loads for a COM class, which apps can use to run code in Explorer
It writes a service's or driver's settings in the registry directly, which can stop Windows from starting; Set-Service is the safer way to change how a service starts

about: Screen steps: setting one control in an app's window. `screen.look` names the app as a name in `apps` (started by its `aumid` when it has no window), as ms-settings: and one of `settings.pages` (always opened at that page), or as the full path of an .exe under `roots` and not under `notRoots` (folders inside Windows that any user can write to and run from), which is only used when it is already open and never started, since a look is a read and starting a program can be a change; folded like a command's name. Rig starts nothing else. Anything else is refused with `words.app`. An image whose file name is in a `refuse` entry, or starts with one of `refuseStarts.starts`, is refused with that entry's `says`, by the app's name before anything is started and again by the window's own image before anything in it is read or pressed. `examples` holds one line per rule for the app's and the helper's tests.

A window's program is a listed app (`apps`, `settings`) only when its file name is the app's `image`, its full path starts with one of the app's `folders`, and it runs as one of the app's packages (`families`, which name the publisher) or, outside C:\Program Files\WindowsApps, unpackaged; its signer counts only when it is that package or one of the app's `signers`. A program named by its path counts by that path, and its signer only when it is validly signed and, under C:\Windows, by one of `windowsSigners`. `imageExamples` holds a line per rule for the helper's tests.

A look is clean when the window's program counts as above, its signer counts, it isn't in `contentHosts`, the control it reads and its choices are a Button, CheckBox, ComboBox, ListItem, RadioButton or Slider, and nothing on the way is under a Document control. A screen step is always tier 3, is refused when its look isn't clean, and its `to` must be one of the look's choices or a number in its range.

In Settings nothing is selected, so a walk stays on the page it was opened at. A walk selects only tabs and tree rows, which change what the window shows; it never picks a row of a list or grid, since in some apps that row is the setting itself, nor a row inside a ComboBox. Nothing under a Document control (web content) is ever selected, expanded or pressed. A control whose name holds one of `neverNames` (folded) is never walked through, set or pressed, and no step may set a value named like one. `commit` holds the button names an approved change may press after setting the control: an Apply button, or OK when the window also has a Cancel. Before setting anything the change stops when an Apply button is already enabled (changes are waiting that the card didn't show), and before pressing one it stops when any other control Rig can read has moved. When a button not on these lists became enabled and none on them can be pressed, the change isn't finished and is put back, except in an app marked `appliesOnChange`.

refuse.says: Rig doesn't drive mail or chat apps
Rig doesn't drive terminals or script hosts
Rig doesn't drive Windows' own admin tools
Rig doesn't drive remote control tools
Rig only opens Settings at a page on its list, written ms-settings: and the page's name

refuseStarts.says: Rig doesn't drive installers or uninstallers

words.app: Rig can drive an app it knows by name, a Settings page on its list written ms-settings: and the page's name, or a program named by its full path under C:\Program Files or C:\Windows that is already open
words.not-open: Rig only starts the apps on its own list. Open it yourself, then ask again
words.never-name: Rig doesn't open, set or press anything in an app with a name like that
words.combo-row: That is a choice in a drop-down, and choosing it would change the setting. Name the drop-down itself to read it
words.goal: A look needs the names of one to eight controls to walk to, each a short line of plain text
words.unknown-look: Rig hasn't looked at this control, or looked too long ago. Look again, then ask
words.not-offered: That isn't one of the values the control offered when Rig looked
words.unclean: The window Rig looked at shows text from outside, or isn't a signed program in Program Files or Windows, so Rig won't change it from this chat
words.op: A screen change needs the look it came from, the new value and one sentence that says what it does
words.tier: Rig presses the app's own controls and can't see what the app writes, so putting it back means walking the same path again and can miss
words.not-maker: This window's program isn't the one Rig knows for this app, or isn't signed by its maker, so Rig won't drive it
words.web-content: That part of the app is web content, and Rig only reads it, never presses anything there
words.list-row: That is a row in a list, and in some apps picking a row is the setting itself, so Rig doesn't pick one. Pick it yourself, then ask again
words.waiting: has changes waiting that Rig didn't make. Apply or cancel them there, then ask again
words.minimised: is minimised. Restore its window, then ask again

never.says: Rig never edits sign-in, key or browser profile files

tier3.says: It edits settings a developer tool or coding agent reads, which can name a program for it to run
